title: Application Layer Protocol: Web Protocols
summary:
Web protocols command and control describes adversary use of HTTP and HTTPS to carry instructions and exfiltrated data between an implant and its controller. The traffic is designed to resemble ordinary web browsing: it uses standard ports, valid transport encryption, conventional request methods and headers, and often a legitimate-looking hostname or a domain fronted by a content delivery network. Because the channel is encrypted and rides on the same infrastructure the business depends on, network inspection cannot rely on payload signatures, and detection shifts toward metadata, timing, and behavioural consistency.

Observable artefacts are concentrated in proxy, DNS, TLS, and endpoint data. Proxy logs capture the requested host, full URL path, method, user agent, response size, and byte counts in each direction, and beaconing appears as a strikingly regular interval between requests to the same endpoint from a single internal host, often continuing outside working hours. TLS metadata may reveal a self-signed or unusual certificate, a mismatch between the certificate subject and the requested hostname, or a client that fails to perform expected revocation checks. DNS logs show resolution of the controller domain, sometimes to hosting ranges rather than content networks. On the endpoint, the responsible process is frequently an unexpected binary or a legitimate one with no reason to make network connections, and its command line and file origin provide additional context.

Benign web traffic is the largest data source in any environment and includes software updates, telemetry, and cloud applications, several of which also beacon on fixed intervals. Investigations therefore combine multiple weak signals: an unusual process making regular requests, to a domain with a short registration history, with a consistent user agent that matches no deployed software, and either a long-lived connection or a request pattern that persists through nights and weekends.
objectives: Explain how adversaries shape HTTP and HTTPS traffic to resemble legitimate browsing and why payload inspection fails.
Identify beaconing through interval regularity, byte-size consistency, and persistence outside business hours in proxy logs.
Analyse TLS metadata such as certificate subject, issuer, and validity to surface infrastructure that does not match its hostname.
Correlate endpoint process telemetry with proxy and DNS records to attribute a network connection to a specific binary.
Build baselined detection logic that suppresses known update and cloud application beaconing without losing coverage.
Map web protocol command and control to ATT&CK and describe the value and limits of each mitigation available.

beginner.definition: Web protocols are the rules your browser uses to fetch pages, mainly HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) and its encrypted version HTTPS (Hypertext Transfer Protocol Secure). Attackers can hide their control traffic inside the same rules, so the connection blends into ordinary web browsing. The infected computer looks like it is visiting a website.
beginner.whyItMatters: After breaking in, an attacker needs a way to send orders to the infected machine and receive stolen data back. Web traffic is perfect for that, because almost every network allows it out. The content is encrypted, so nobody can read it, and blocking all web traffic would stop the business. You must therefore look at behaviour, such as a machine calling the same address every few minutes, rather than at the content.
howItWorks: The attacker sets up a server on the internet that will act as the controller.
Malware on the victim machine contacts that server using ordinary web requests.
It asks for new instructions at regular intervals, and this rhythm is called beaconing.
Stolen files are sent back inside normal-looking requests, so they leave the network quietly.
Proxy logs show the regular rhythm, and endpoint logs show which program made the connection.
beginner.example: Think of a spy who hides messages inside ordinary shopping catalogues. The postman delivers them without suspicion, because the catalogue is a normal thing to receive. The spy's handler writes the real orders in code between the furniture photos. Nobody reading the outside of the envelope learns anything. Malicious web traffic works the same way, wrapped in the same requests that load every shopping site you visit.
takeaways: You cannot read encrypted web traffic, so focus on patterns instead of content.
A regular call home every few minutes, day and night, is a classic warning sign.
Match the network connection to the program that made it, because that identifies the malware.
